clue.text: A sight of tobacco from above

definitions.text: A sight of tobacco from above

parts.words: A sight of tobacco from above
parts.note: Bird's-eye is a brand of pipe tobacco and a view is a sight, so the phrase for a high overhead view reads as a look at that tobacco

explanation.surface: Someone looks down on a heap of pipe tobacco.
explanation.walkthrough: Bird's-eye was a well-known cut of pipe tobacco, so a view of it doubles as the name for an aerial view.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means a panorama seen from high overhead, as a flying creature would see the ground.

clue.text: Little devils tradition

parts.note: an imp is a little devil and lore is tradition; together they make a verb meaning to beg, which the clue leaves the solver to supply

explanation.surface: A custom passed down among mischievous sprites.
explanation.walkthrough: This old clue gives only the pieces, IMP (little devil) and LORE (tradition), with no separate definition; the solver joins them into the word for pleading.
explanation.definitionFit: Joining a small fiend with folklore spells a common verb meaning to entreat or beg earnestly.

clue.text: A reckless chap, he challenged sin

parts.note: to challenge someone is to dare them; he dared
sin is evil

explanation.surface: A rash young man who went so far as to defy wickedness.
explanation.definitionFit: A daredevil is a person who takes foolhardy risks, a bold and rash fellow.

clue.text: Right of way

parts.note: in law a right of way across another's land is the classic example of this kind of entitlement

explanation.walkthrough: The clue is a plain example: a legal right to cross someone else's land is the standard instance of this property right.
explanation.definitionFit: In property law it is a right held over another person's land, such as passage along a path.

clue.text: A letter to a niece provides a name for her

indicators.note: the letter and the niece together provide a new arrangement of their letters

parts.note: U is a letter of the alphabet (and sounds like 'you', the one written to)

explanation.surface: Writing to a niece supplies a name for her.
explanation.walkthrough: Add the letter U to NIECE and rearrange the six letters.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a female given name, found in the New Testament as the mother of Timothy.

clue.text: If the bulbs aren't in the lamp they may be here

definitions.text: If the bulbs aren't in the lamp they may be here

parts.words: If the bulbs aren't in the lamp they may be here
parts.note: bulbs suggest light bulbs, but plant bulbs are planted in a flower bed, and a person not up with a lamp is asleep there too

explanation.surface: Light bulbs missing from a lamp have been put away somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bulbs' and 'lamp' point to electric lighting; the bulbs are those of tulips and the like, which live in a garden bed.
explanation.definitionFit: Flower bulbs are planted in a garden plot, so when not in a lamp they would be found planted there.

clue.text: May the illuminations grow!

parts.note: to wax is to grow and lights are illuminations, so the wish 'lights, wax!' names candles of wax

explanation.surface: A toast that festive light displays should get bigger.
explanation.walkthrough: Wax means grow, as the moon waxes, and lights are illuminations; read together they name candles.
explanation.definitionFit: These are wax candles or tapers, a source of illumination made from beeswax or paraffin.

clue.text: A naval flow

parts.note: the Flow in Orkney that served as the Royal Navy's main anchorage

explanation.walkthrough: Scapa Flow is a sheltered stretch of sea in the Orkney Islands, off northern Scotland, used as Britain's chief naval base in both world wars.
explanation.definitionFit: The name completes the Orkney anchorage famous as a fleet base and the scene of the German fleet's scuttling in 1919.

clue.text: Time's up (anag.)

parts.note: the clue gives only the fodder and tells the solver to rearrange it; the letters of time's up make a word for driving force

explanation.walkthrough: An old-style clue with no definition: rearrange the letters of TIMESUP into a real word.
explanation.definitionFit: The result means momentum or a driving force that sets something moving.

clue.text: A knight returned in a fowl

definitions.text: A knight returned in a fowl

parts.words: A knight returned in a fowl
parts.note: a capon is a fowl; inside it go A and SIR, the knight's title, turned round as RIS, giving a word for a horse's ornamented covering

explanation.surface: A knight comes back stuffed inside a chicken.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue gives only wordplay: CAPON (a fowl) with A plus RIS (SIR, a knight's title, turned back) inside. The result is a knight's horse's trappings, so the knight is apt.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the decorated cloth covering spread over a horse, especially a knight's charger.

clue.text: Wenches seem often to have been

definitions.text: Wenches seem often to have been

parts.words: Wenches seem often to have been
parts.note: in old ballads and tales the serving wench is stock-described as plump and full-bosomed

explanation.walkthrough: The clue relies on the literary stereotype of the tavern wench as plump and comely.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means plump and full-figured, the stock epithet of rosy country girls in old literature.

clue.text: Nor you, impute to these the fault If Memory o'er their tomb no trophies raise " (Gray)

definitions.text: Nor you, impute to these the fault If Memory o'er their tomb no trophies raise " (Gray)

parts.words: Nor you, impute to these the fault If Memory o'er their tomb no trophies raise " (Gray)
parts.note: a quotation from Gray's Elegy with a word missing after 'Nor you, ye'; the missing word addresses the haughty

explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Gray's 'Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard' reads 'Nor you, ye ___, impute to these the fault'; the solver supplies the missing word.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing epithet names the haughty and grand, contrasted in the poem with the humble village dead.

clue.text: Came in ode (anag.)

parts.note: the clue gives only the fodder and tells the solver to rearrange the letters of came in ode into a culinary word

explanation.walkthrough: An old-style clue with no definition: rearrange CAMEINODE.
explanation.definitionFit: The result is a dish of mixed diced vegetables or fruit, often set in jelly.

clue.text: Like deer

parts.note: a plain definition: the Latin-based adjective for anything resembling or relating to stags and hinds

explanation.definitionFit: From Latin cervus, a stag, the adjective describes things relating to or resembling these animals.

clue.text: It's a little sweet

parts.note: a small scented lozenge sucked to sweeten the breath

explanation.walkthrough: 'A little sweet' could mean slightly sugary; here it is a small sweet, a breath lozenge.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a tiny aromatic pastille taken to freshen the breath, a small confection.

clue.text: He doesn't look on the wine when it is red, but the next best thing

definitions.text: He doesn't look on the wine when it is red, but the next best thing

parts.words: He doesn't look on the wine when it is red, but the next best thing
parts.note: echoing Proverbs 23:31, 'Look not thou upon the wine when it is red'; this official inspected beer instead

explanation.walkthrough: The clue twists the biblical warning against wine; the officer in question was a manorial inspector who tested the quality of ale.
explanation.definitionFit: This was a borough officer appointed to test ale sold in his district, checking its quality and measure.

clue.text: Mrs. Malaprop's diagram, perhaps

parts.note: Mrs Malaprop, from Sheridan's The Rivals, misuses words; her 'diagram' would be the diaphragm, which is this part of the body

explanation.walkthrough: Mrs Malaprop is the character in Sheridan's play The Rivals who swaps similar-sounding words, so her 'diagram' is a diaphragm.
explanation.definitionFit: The diaphragm is the muscular partition across the middle of the trunk, and this word names that region.

clue.text: Ten heard, but only one was faithful

indicators.note: a loose old-style signal: the words ten heard, but put otherwise, giving their letters in a new order

parts.note: the letters of ten heard are the fodder

explanation.surface: Ten people listened, but just one stayed loyal.
explanation.walkthrough: This 1945 clue signals the rearrangement only loosely with 'but'; reshuffle TENHEARD. 'Only one was' points to a single follower among the ten listeners.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective it means sticking fast or loyal, as a follower who holds to a cause.

clue.text: A simple revision

parts.note: revising the letters of simple gives a verb meaning drives forward

explanation.walkthrough: An old-style clue with no definition: rework the letters of SIMPLE into a real word.
explanation.definitionFit: The result means drives or urges forward, as a force propels something.

clue.text: A botanical little pan ?

parts.note: the word has the look of a cooking vessel with a diminutive ending, but it is a term from plant science for a kind of flower head

explanation.walkthrough: The word looks like PAN plus the diminutive ending -ICLE, as in 'particle', but it is a botanical term.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a loose, branching cluster of flowers, as found on oats or lilac.

clue.text: A spell of idleness long ago

definitions.text: A spell of idleness long ago

parts.words: A spell of idleness long ago
parts.note: the archaic, poetic word for idleness, used in Spenser and older verse

explanation.walkthrough: 'A spell of' suggests a period of time; it means a way of spelling the word, the old poetic form.
explanation.definitionFit: This archaic literary term means a state of lazy ease, used by older poets.

clue.text: There seems to be no opposition in this case

definitions.text: There seems to be no opposition in this case

parts.words: There seems to be no opposition in this case
parts.note: the Latin abbreviation for 'with nobody contradicting', used of a unanimous vote

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is short for Latin nemine contradicente, 'no one speaking against', so it describes a vote passed unopposed.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the abbreviated Latin phrase recorded when a motion passes unanimously, with no dissenter.

clue.text: This relation would need a wash if he were eventually' articled

definitions.text: This relation would need a wash if he were eventually' articled

parts.words: This relation would need a wash if he were eventually' articled
parts.note: add the article 'an' at the end of this relative and he becomes dirty, in need of washing

explanation.walkthrough: 'Articled' sounds like a trainee lawyer's status; here it means given an article, AN, at the end, which turns the relative into UNCLEAN.
explanation.definitionFit: This family member is a parent's brother, a relation who becomes unwashed when an article is tacked on.

clue.text: King John may have thought the drink a bit thin

definitions.text: King John may have thought the drink a bit thin

parts.words: King John may have thought the drink a bit thin
parts.note: a watery mead would be runny mead, and King John sealed Magna Carta in 1215 at the riverside meadow of that name

explanation.walkthrough: King John sealed Magna Carta at the meadow beside the Thames whose name sounds like 'runny mead', a thin honey wine.
explanation.definitionFit: The meadow near Windsor where Magna Carta was sealed in 1215 is famously linked to that king.

clue.text: He thought at night

parts.note: the poet is named for the title of his long 18th-century meditative poem about thoughts by night

explanation.walkthrough: Edward Young was an 18th-century English poet best known for 'Night Thoughts'.
explanation.definitionFit: The poet's surname fits because his famous work is a meditation in verse composed of thoughts by night.

clue.text: Did he use the brush ?

parts.note: the surname of an Irish portrait painter splits into a question offering an alternative to the brush

explanation.walkthrough: Sir William Orpen was a celebrated Irish portrait and war painter; his name splits as 'or pen', the alternative to the brush.
explanation.definitionFit: The painter's surname reads as an alternative writing tool, so asking about his brush is apt.

clue.text: Who is President of the Regimental Institutes? am, — and hang the grammar

definitions.text: Who is President of the Regimental Institutes? am, — and hang the grammar

parts.words: Who is President of the Regimental Institutes? am, — and hang the grammar
parts.note: PRI is the army abbreviation for President of the Regimental Institutes; asked who is PRI, the ungrammatical reply is 'me'

explanation.walkthrough: PRI stands for President of the Regimental Institutes; answering 'PRI? Me!' ignores grammar and gives the word meaning first-rate.
explanation.definitionFit: The joined pieces make a word meaning best or first in rank, though the clue gives no separate definition.

clue.text: This will be found in the milk if I churn it

indicators.note: the letters will be found inside the run of words if I churn, read straight through

explanation.surface: Churning milk turns up something unexpected.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This' refers to the answer itself; 'the milk' only sets the dairy scene, and the word sits inside 'if I churn'.
explanation.definitionFit: A fichu is a light triangular scarf for the neck, and 'This' stands for it as the thing hidden.

clue.text: This should be introduced, of course, by an impeccable Minister

definitions.text: This should be introduced, of course, by an impeccable Minister

parts.words: This should be introduced, of course, by an impeccable Minister
parts.note: a minister introduces legislation in Parliament, and an impeccable one would bring in spotless legislation, also the phrase for a good report of health

explanation.walkthrough: A minister introduces a bill to Parliament; an untainted minister's bill would be a clean one, as in 'clean bill of health'.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a certificate of good health or a clear record, here pictured as a spotless piece of legislation.

clue.text: … having, no doubt, first steamed on to the table

definitions.text: … having, no doubt, first steamed on to the table

parts.words: … having, no doubt, first steamed on to the table
parts.note: jokingly, something that steamed to the table like a locomotive and was turned there

explanation.walkthrough: Engine-turning is a decoration of fine machine-cut patterns on watch cases and silver; the clue pictures a steam engine arriving at the turntable.
explanation.definitionFit: The term describes metal ornamented with intricate lines cut by a lathe, a common finish on cigarette cases.
